# What is Quarto?

-   **Quarto** is a next-generation tool for creating dynamic, reproducible documents.
-   It lets you combine:
    -   Text (Markdown)
    -   Code (R, Python, Julia, etc.)
    -   Outputs (plots, tables, results)
-   Think of it as *R Markdown 2.0* — more powerful, flexible, and language-agnostic.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Why use Quarto for reports?

-   Integrates seamlessly with **RStudio**
-   Encourages **reproducible research**\
    → All your code, results, and text in one file\
-   Easily export to:
    -   HTML (interactive reports)
    -   PDF (formal reports)
    -   Word (submission-ready)
-   Supports version control (Git/GitHub)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Getting started

1.  Open **RStudio**
2.  Go to:\
    **File → New File → Quarto Document**
3.  Choose a format (HTML, PDF, or Word)
4.  Save your file with the extension:\
    `.qmd`

# Structuring your report

Headings control the hierarchy of your document.\
In Markdown (and Quarto), they’re made with the `#` symbol.

**Markdown syntax:**

``` markdown
# This is a top-level heading
# This is a second-level heading
## This is a third-level heading
## This is a fourth-level heading
```

**Rendered output:**

<p style="font-size:1.8em; font-weight:bold;">This is a top-level heading</p>
<p style="font-size:1.5em; font-weight:bold;">This is a second-level heading</p>
<p style="font-size:1.3em; font-weight:bold;">This is a third-level heading</p>
<p style="font-size:1.1em; font-weight:bold;">This is a fourth-level heading</p>

💡 Use `#` for main sections (e.g. *Introduction*, *Results*), and add more `#` for subsections.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Text formatting and emphasis

Use simple Markdown symbols to style your writing.

**Markdown syntax:**

``` markdown
*italic text*
**bold text**
***bold and italic***
- Bullet list item
1. Numbered list item
```

**Rendered output:**

*italic text*\
**bold text**\
***bold and italic***

-   Bullet list item
-   Bullet list item 2

1.  Numbered list item\
2.  Numbered list item 2

💡 You can also mix formatting in text, e.g.\
*The **results** show a strong correlation.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The basic structure of a `.qmd` file

A simple Quarto document has three parts:

1.  **YAML header** — defines document metadata (title, author, format), encased with `---`
2.  **Markdown text** — where you write your report
3.  **Code chunks** — where you include R/Python code and outputs

## Example

**Markdown syntax:**

![](images/clipboard-1861789580.png)

**Rendered output:**

<h1 class="toc-ignore">

Introduction

</h1>

This is where your text goes

```{r}
summary(cars)
```

🧩 **Explanation:** - The lines between `---` at the top form the **YAML header** - Headings like `# Introduction` create report sections - Code chunks are written between triple backticks with `{r}` to indicate R code. Note that in the rendered example, I used `## introduction` because I didn't want it to mess with the toc.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Understanding code chunks

A code chunk starts with three backticks followed by `{r}`, and ends with three backticks.

**Markdown syntax:**

![](images/clipboard-2117407583.png)

**Rendered output:**

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
head(starwars)
```

💡 Options can be added after `#|`, for example:

-   `echo: false` → hide code\
-   `warning: false` → suppress warnings\
-   `fig-cap:` → add figure caption

For example:

![](images/clipboard-3755537326.png)

Will give the `head()` of the starwars dataset, but without explicitly printing the code to the document.

```{r}
#| echo: false
head(starwars)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Creating plots with R code chunks

You can insert a code chunk in RStudio with:

**Shortcut:**\
- <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>Alt</kbd> + <kbd>I</kbd> (Windows/Linux)\
- <kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Option</kbd> + <kbd>I</kbd> (Mac)

or manually type:

![](images/clipboard-2293103632.png)

We can fill those code chunks with plot code, and the plots will automatically render into the document:

**Markdown syntax:**

![](images/clipboard-4754547.png)


**Rendered output:**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "A basic plot created in Quarto"
plot(pressure)
```

💡 When you **render** your Quarto document, this code runs automatically and the plot appears below it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Hiding code but showing plots

If you only want to show the *plot*, not the *code*, use:

**Markdown syntax:**

`#| echo: false`

**Rendered output:**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Plot output only"
plot(pressure)
```

💡 Use this for your final report when you want to display polished results without showing the underlying code.

------------------------------------------------------------------------


# Adding external figures

You can easily include images and figures that are **stored outside your Quarto document** — such as `.png`, `.jpg`, `.svg`, or `.pdf` files.

---

## Basic Markdown image syntax

The simplest way to add an image is with standard Markdown:

```markdown
![Caption describing the image](images/plot1.png)
```

- `![ ]` — contains the figure caption  
- `( )` — contains the file path  
- If your image is in the same folder as your `.qmd` file, you can just use the file name (e.g. `figure1.png`).
- You can also add images with URLs, but this is poor practice RE reproducibility
- If you do this, you'll have to add `embed-resources: true` in your YAML header to ensure everything is packaged in a single place.

```markdown
![Happiest dog in the world](https://a-z-animals.com/media/2021/04/happy-golden-retriever-3-1024x819.jpg)
```

![Happiest dog in the world](https://a-z-animals.com/media/2021/04/happy-golden-retriever-3-1024x819.jpg)

---


## Supported image formats

| Format | Description | Notes |
|---------|--------------|-------|
| `.png` | Portable Network Graphics | Good for raster plots (ggplot, base R) |
| `.jpg` | JPEG | Compressed, smaller files, less crisp |
| `.svg` | Scalable Vector Graphics | Perfect for line art and vector graphics |
| `.pdf` | Portable Document Format | High quality, ideal for publication figures |

---

## Controlling figure layout in reports

You can arrange multiple images side-by-side using Pandoc’s **columns** syntax:

```markdown
::::{.columns}
::: column
![](images/fig1.png){fig-cap="Figure A" width=100%}
:::
::: column
![](images/fig2.png){fig-cap="Figure B" width=100%}
:::
::::
```

💡 This creates a two-column layout — useful for comparing plots or panels.

---


## Recommended workflow

1. Create an `/images` folder in your project directory  
2. Save or export all figures to this folder  
3. Reference them in your `.qmd` file with relative paths:
   ```markdown
   ![](images/my_figure.png){fig-cap="My figure caption"}
   ```
4. Keep filenames short and descriptive (e.g. `plot_speed_dist.png`)

# Adding tables

Tables in Quarto can be created in two main ways:  
1. **Manually**, using Markdown syntax  
2. **Automatically**, using R code outputs

---

## Basic Markdown tables

You can write tables directly in Markdown using `|` and `-` characters to define columns and headers.

```markdown
| Species | Mass (g) | Wingspan (cm) |
|----------|-----------|---------------|
| Sparrow  | 24        | 21            |
| Starling | 78        | 34            |
| Crow     | 320       | 84            |
```

**Rendered output:**

| Species | Mass (g) | Wingspan (cm) |
|----------|-----------|---------------|
| Sparrow  | 24        | 21            |
| Starling | 78        | 34            |
| Crow     | 320       | 84            |

💡 Tip: You can align text by adding `:` —  
`:---` (left), `:---:` (center), `---:` (right).

---

## Creating tables with R code


Quarto supports several R packages that produce attractive, formatted tables in your reports.  
These tables update automatically whenever you re-render your document.

---

## Using `knitr::kable()`

The simplest way to make a polished table is with **`knitr::kable()`**.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of car speeds and distances"
library(knitr)
kable(head(cars), caption = "First six rows of the cars dataset")
```

**Rendered output:**  
A clean, lightweight table — perfect for HTML or PDF reports.

---

## Using `gt` for professional-quality tables

The **`gt`** package gives you full control over table styling, alignment, and formatting.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Formatted table using gt"
library(gt)
cars %>%
  head(10) %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Speed and Stopping Distance",
    subtitle = "Sample from the cars dataset"
  ) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(speed, dist), decimals = 1)
```

💡 `gt` automatically applies nice fonts, spacing, and captions.  
It’s the best option for HTML output.

---

## Using `flextable` (great for Word documents)

If your students will render reports to Word (`.docx`), `flextable` produces tables that remain editable in Word.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Flextable example"
library(flextable)
flextable(head(cars))
```

✅ Works beautifully in **Word** and **PDF** outputs.  
💡 Requires `officer` and `flextable` packages to be installed.

---

## Styling and captions

- Use `#| tbl-cap:` in the chunk options to add a caption automatically  
- You can also add a manual caption using the function argument (e.g. `caption = "..."` in `kable()`)  
- Each table type supports cross-referencing with labels (e.g. `#tbl-cars`)

---

## Summary

| Method | Best for | Appearance | Key function |
|---------|-----------|-------------|---------------|
| `knitr::kable()` | Simple, fast | Clean default HTML/PDF | `kable()` |
| `gt` | Professional reports | Highly styled, customisable | `gt()` |
| `flextable` | Word documents | Editable and neat | `flextable()` |

# Citing references

You can add a bibliography in your YAML header if you want...

**Markdown syntax:**

``` markdown
---
title: "My Report"
bibliography: references.bib
---
```

Then cite in text with `@citationkey`, e.g.:

> Quarto supports citations just like R Markdown [@knuth1984].

Render your report:

``` bash
quarto render myreport.qmd
```

This is quite involved, and probably not useful for your LIFE4138 coursework. If you want to use it another time and get stuck, let me know! 🤩

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Rendering your report

## In RStudio

-   Click the **Render** button (top toolbar)

-   Or run in console:

    ``` r
    quarto::quarto_render("myreport.qmd")
    ```

## Output options

**Markdown syntax:**

``` markdown
format:
  html: default
  pdf: default
  docx: default
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Customising appearance

You can style your document with:

-   **Themes:** `theme: cosmo`, `theme: flatly`, `theme: journal`
-   **Code highlighting:** `highlight-style: github`
-   **TOC and section numbering:**

**Markdown syntax:**

``` markdown
toc: true
number-sections: true
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Common mistakes to avoid

-   ❌ Missing or unbalanced `---` in YAML\
-   ❌ Using tabs instead of spaces in YAML\
-   ❌ Forgetting to close code chunks\
-   ❌ Using R Markdown syntax like `{r, echo=TRUE}` (no comma syntax in Quarto)

✅ Use Quarto-style chunk options with `#|`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Summary

🎯 Quarto helps you:

-   Write **reproducible, dynamic reports**
-   Integrate **R code and outputs**
-   Produce **professional documents** in any format
-   Transition seamlessly from R Markdown
